sections.title: Special Rules for Degrees of Comparison
sections.content: Step 1: Check if the Adjective is showing comparison (taller, more beautiful). Step 2: Some Adjectives take a specific preposition — senior to, junior to, superior to, inferior to (always 'to', never 'than'). Step 3: Preferable, preferable to; prefer A to B ('prefer than' is wrong). Step 4: Avoid double comparisons — 'more better', 'most highest' are wrong.

sections.title: Relative Pronouns (who, whom, which, that)
sections.content: Step 1: A Relative Pronoun describes the Noun (antecedent) that comes before it. Step 2: If the antecedent is a person and the pronoun is acting as the subject → who. Step 3: If it is acting as an object → whom (even after a preposition, use whom). Step 4: For things/animals, use 'which'; 'that' can also be used in defining clauses.

sections.title: Correlative Conjunctions and Subject-Verb Agreement
sections.content: Step 1: Identify the pair — Either...or, Neither...nor, Not only...but also. Step 2: The verb will always agree with the second subject (the subject closer to the verb). Step 3: If the second subject is singular, the verb is singular; if plural, the verb is plural. Step 4: Keep the structure balanced — Either Ram or his friends are coming.

sections.title: Position of Adverbs (only, enough, too)
sections.content: Step 1: Place 'Only' right before the word it limits. Step 2: 'Enough' comes after an adjective (tall enough), but before a noun (enough money). Step 3: 'Too' means excessive amount and comes before an adjective/adverb (too hot). Step 4: A wrong position can change the meaning.

sections.title: Confusing Prepositions (in vs into, beside vs besides)
sections.content: Step 1: 'In' indicates position or location, 'into' indicates movement. Step 2: If there is an action of going inside → into; if already inside → in. Step 3: 'Beside' means next to; 'Besides' means in addition to. Step 4: Choose the right preposition by understanding the meaning of the sentence.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content: 1. Writing 'senior than' (wrong). 2. Using 'who' instead of 'whom' for objects. 3. Matching the verb with the first subject in Either...or structures. 4. Changing the sentence's meaning due to the wrong placement of 'only'. 5. Confusion between 'in' and 'into'.

sections.title: Quick Summary
sections.content: Remember the correct prepositions in comparisons. Choose the Relative Pronoun based on its role (subject vs object). In correlative conjunctions, match the verb with the closer subject. The correct position of an Adverb clarifies the meaning. Prepositions depend heavily on context and movement.

tricks.title: Senior/Junior Trick
tricks.explanation: Step 1: If you see senior, junior, superior, inferior. Step 2: Immediately remember 'to'. Step 3: Never use 'than'.

tricks.title: Prefer Trick
tricks.explanation: Step 1: If there are two things being compared with prefer. Step 2: Structure: prefer A to B. Step 3: Do not use 'than'.

tricks.title: Who vs Whom Trick
tricks.explanation: Step 1: Find the verb in the clause. Step 2: If the pronoun is the subject performing the verb → who. Step 3: If it is the object receiving the action → whom.
tricks.example: The man whom I met was kind.

tricks.title: Either/Neither Agreement Trick
tricks.explanation: Step 1: Identify the two subjects. Step 2: Match the verb with the closer subject. Step 3: Check the number (singular/plural).
tricks.example: Either the teacher or the students are ready.

tricks.title: Not Only Structure Trick
tricks.explanation: Step 1: Subject after 'Not only'. Step 2: Parallel structure after 'but also'. Step 3: Verb agrees with the closer subject.
tricks.example: Not only Ram but also his friends are coming.

tricks.title: Only Position Trick
tricks.explanation: Step 1: Identify the word 'Only' is limiting. Step 2: Place it right before that word. Step 3: Check how the meaning shifts.
tricks.example: She only eats fruits. (Means she does nothing else but eat them.)

tricks.title: Enough Trick
tricks.explanation: Step 1: Use 'Enough' after an Adjective. Step 2: Use 'Enough' before a Noun. Step 3: The meaning is 'sufficient'.
tricks.example: He is tall enough. We have enough food.

tricks.title: Too Trick
tricks.explanation: Step 1: Too = more than needed/excessive. Step 2: Place before an adjective/adverb. Step 3: Often carries a negative sense.
tricks.example: It is too cold to swim.

tricks.title: In vs Into Trick
tricks.explanation: Step 1: Is there movement from outside to inside? Then 'into'. Step 2: Is it a static position? Then 'in'. Step 3: Identify the action verb.
tricks.example: She went into the room. She is in the room.

tricks.title: Beside vs Besides Trick
tricks.explanation: Step 1: Need the meaning 'next to'? Use beside. Step 2: Need the meaning 'in addition to'? Use besides. Step 3: Check the sentence's context.
tricks.example: He sat beside me. Besides English, he knows Hindi.
